title: Psalm 87: Born in Zion
summary: The LORD has founded his city on the holy mountains and loves the gates of Zion above every other dwelling in Israel. In a startling oracle, God names Israel's old enemies and distant peoples (Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Cush) among those who know him and records them in his register as born in Zion. The psalm ends with singers and dancers declaring that all their springs of joy are in her.
story: Psalm 87 is one of the Korahite psalms near the end of Book III and one of the Songs of Zion, the psalms that celebrate Jerusalem as the city where God chose to dwell (compare Psalms 46, 48, and 84). It follows the prayer of Psalm 86, where David declared that all the nations God made will come and bow before him, and it gives that hope a concrete shape: the nations are not merely conquered or brought to bow but are enrolled as citizens of God's city. It sits just before the darkest psalm in the Psalter (Psalm 88) and the lament over David's line (Psalm 89), so the reader carries this wide vision of Zion into the book's collapse. The promise that God made to Abraham, that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3), stands in the background.
historical:
The heading ascribes the psalm to the sons of Korah, the Levitical singers of the temple, and calls it both a psalm and a song. As with other headings, scholars debate whether this reflects authorship or the collection it was drawn from.

The psalm's date is uncertain. Babylon's presence in the list has led some to place it after the rise of the Neo-Babylonian empire in the late seventh century BC or even after the exile, when Jewish communities were scattered through Egypt, Babylon, and beyond. Others think a pre-exilic date is possible, since Babylon was an ancient and famous city long before it became Judah's conqueror, and they connect the psalm with the confidence in Zion found in Isaiah, whose prophecies include Egypt and Assyria worshiping alongside Israel (Isaiah 19:23-25) and the nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD (Isaiah 2:2-4). The psalm names no event, and its short, compressed Hebrew makes firm dating difficult.
cultural:
The five peoples named in verse 4 cover the ancient world Israel knew. Rahab here is not the woman of Jericho but a poetic name for Egypt, drawn from the name of a sea monster that represented chaos (Isaiah 30:7 uses it this way; Psalm 89:10 speaks of God crushing Rahab). Babylon was the great power to the east. Philistia was Israel's old rival on the southwestern coast, Tyre the wealthy Phoenician trading city to the north, and Cush the land south of Egypt along the upper Nile, roughly modern Sudan, which stood in Israelite imagination for the far edge of the world. Egypt and Babylon were the two empires that had enslaved or exiled Israel.

Cities in the ancient world kept registers of citizens, and in Israel genealogical lists recorded who belonged to which tribe and family (Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 record the returning exiles by family, and some who could not prove their descent were excluded, Ezra 2:62). Birth determined citizenship, rights, and belonging. In Psalm 87 God himself keeps the register, and he writes foreigners in as native-born. Verse 7 pictures a festival procession with singers and pipers or dancers (the Hebrew verb can mean to play the flute or to dance), and springs were a common image of life and blessing flowing from the place of God's presence.
literary: Psalm 87 is a brief hymn of Zion, compressed and in places difficult to translate. It moves in three short scenes. Verses 1 to 3 praise the city God founded and loves, ending with Selah (a musical or liturgical marker of uncertain meaning). Verses 4 to 6 contain God's oracle and its echo: God speaks in the first person in verse 4, the community repeats the claim in verse 5, and God records it in verse 6. The refrain “This one was born in Zion” appears three times in slightly different forms, and the repetition works like a legal declaration read out and entered in the record. Verse 7 ends with the celebration of the citizens. Rahab and Babylon, named first in verse 4, are precisely the powers the reader would least expect to hear enrolled.

outline.t: The city God founded and loves
The nations registered as born in Zion
All my springs of joy are in you

doctrines.note: Zion here is the gathered people of God, a city whose citizens come from every nation and belong because God declares that they do. The psalm anticipates a people of God defined by his registration rather than by ethnic descent.
God's purpose for Zion was never limited to Israel. The psalm pictures former enemies and distant peoples coming to know the LORD and being counted as his own.
God founds, loves, and establishes his city. Its security and its growth come from him, not from its walls or its kings.

words.note: Yalad, to bear or be born. It appears three times in the refrain. Birth was the basis of citizenship and belonging in the ancient world; to say someone was born in Zion was to say they had full rights there. The psalm uses that language for people born elsewhere, which is its central surprise.

Rahab, literally arrogance or storm. It is the name of a mythical sea monster that Israel's poets used as a symbol of chaos and, by extension, as a nickname for Egypt, the proud power that had enslaved Israel. It is unrelated in Hebrew to the name of Rahab of Jericho.

Katav, to write. In verse 6 God records the peoples in a register. The image of God's book, in which his people's names are written, runs through Scripture (Exodus 32:32; Daniel 12:1) and reaches its fullest form in the book of life in Revelation.

christ: The New Testament takes up the psalm's vision of a city whose citizens are born into it by God's declaration. Paul contrasts the present Jerusalem with “the Jerusalem above”, which he calls the mother of believers (Galatians 4:26). Hebrews tells Christians that they have come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the assembly of the firstborn whose names are written in heaven (Hebrews 12:22-23). Paul tells Gentile believers that they are no longer foreigners but fellow citizens with the saints (Ephesians 2:19). Jesus himself speaks of a new birth by which people enter God's kingdom (John 3:3-5). The psalm did not predict these passages word for word, but the pattern it describes, outsiders enrolled as native-born by God's own act, is exactly what the New Testament says happens through Christ, and the crowd at Pentecost gathered from Egypt, the regions of Babylon's old empire, and beyond (Acts 2:9-11) shows it beginning.

hard.q: Does the psalm mean that foreign nations become part of God's people, or something else?
hard.a:
The Hebrew of verses 4 to 6 is terse, and interpreters read it in more than one way. The most common reading, held widely by both Jewish and Christian scholars, is that the psalm envisions people of other nations coming to know the LORD and being counted as full citizens of Zion, in line with Isaiah's visions of the nations worshiping in Jerusalem. On this reading “those who know Me” refers to foreigners who have come to acknowledge Israel's God.

A second reading takes the verses to refer to Jews of the dispersion, Israelites born in Egypt, Babylon, or Tyre, whom God counts as born in Zion wherever they actually lived. This view points out that large Jewish communities lived in those places after the exile. A third view sees both at once: the scattered people of God and the nations who join them. The first reading best explains the surprise of naming Rahab and Babylon, Israel's oppressors, but the text is short enough that careful readers continue to differ.

questions: The psalm names Israel's oppressors as future citizens of Zion. Whom would you find it hardest to see written into God's register?
Belonging in the ancient world depended on birth. What determines whether someone belongs in your community or church, and how does this psalm challenge that?
Verse 7 says “All my springs of joy are in You.” Where do you actually look for joy, and what would it mean for it to be found in God's city and people?
